source_text: Τί οὖν ὡς καινὸν καὶ ἴδιον θεοῦ παραγγέλλει καὶ μόνον ζωοποιοῦν, ὃ τοὺς προτέρους οὐκ ἔσωσεν; εἰ δὲ ἐξαίρετόν τι ἡ »καινὴ κτίσις«, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, μηνύει καὶ διδάσκει, οὐ τὸ φαινόμενον, ὅπερ ἄλλοι πεποιήκασι, παρεγγυᾷ, ἀλλ᾿ ἕτερόν τι διὰ τούτου σημαινόμενον μεῖζον καὶ θειότερον καὶ τελεώτερον, τὸ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτὴν καὶ τὴν διάθεσιν γυμνῶσαι τῶν ὑπόντων παθῶν καὶ πρόρριζα τὰ ἀλλότρια τῆς γνώμης ἐκτεμεῖν καὶ ἐκβαλεῖν. τοῦτο γὰρ ἴδιον μὲν τοῦ πιστοῦ τὸ μάθημα. ἄξιον δὲ τοῦ σωτῆρος τὸ δίδαγμα. οἱ γάρ τοι πρότεροι, καταφρονήσαντες τῶν ἐκτός, τὰ μὲν κτήματα ἀφῆκαν καὶ παραπώλεσαν, τὰ δὲ πάθη τῶν ψυχῶν οἶμαι ὅτι καὶ προσεπέτειναν· ἐν ὑπεροψίᾳ γὰρ ἐγένοντο καὶ ἀλαζονείᾳ καὶ κενοδοξίᾳ καὶ περιφρονήσει τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων ὡς αὐτοί τι ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον ἐργασάμενοι. πῶς ἂν οὖν ὁ σωτὴρ παρῄνει τοῖς εἰς ἀεὶ βιωσομένοις τὰ βλάψοντα καὶ λυμανούμενα πρὸς τὴν ζωήν, ἣν ἐπαγγέλλεται; καὶ γὰρ αὖ κἀκεῖνό ἐστι· δύναταί τις ἀποφορτισάμενος τὴν κτῆσιν οὐδὲν ἧττον ἔτι τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν καὶ τὴν ὄρεξιν τῶν χρημάτων ἔχειν ἐντετηκυῖαν καὶ συζῶσαν καὶ τὴν μὲν χρῆσιν ἀποβεβληκέναι, ἀπορῶν δὲ ἅμα καὶ ποθῶν ἅπερ ἐσπάθησε διπλῇ λυπεῖσθαι, καὶ τῇ τῆς ὑπηρεσίας ἀπουσίᾳ καὶ τῇ τῆς μετανοίας συνουσίᾳ. ἀνέφικτον γὰρ καὶ ἀμήχανον δεόμενον τῶν πρὸς τὸ βιοτεύειν ἀναγκαίων μὴ οὐ κατακλᾶσθαι τὴν γνώμην καὶ ἀσχολίαν ἄγειν ἀπὸ τῶν κρειττόνων, ὁπωσοῦν καὶ ὁθενοῦν ταῦτα πειρώμενον ἐκπορίζειν.
thought_title: The new creation teaches stripping the soul, not the body
orientation: Clement is arguing that Jesus' command to sell possessions is not about outward poverty, which pagans already practiced, but about a new, divine teaching that strips the soul of passions.
pass_a_gloss: Why then does he command as something new and proper to God and alone life-giving, which did not save the former people? But if the new creation, the Son of God, reveals and teaches something exceptional, he does not command the visible thing, which others have done, but something else signified through this, greater and more divine and more complete: to strip the soul itself and the disposition of the passions that are present in it and to cut out and cast out root and branch the things alien to the judgment. For this is the lesson proper to the believer. And the teaching is worthy of the Savior. For indeed the former people, despising external things, gave up and squandered their possessions, but the passions of their souls, I think, they even increased; for they came to be in arrogance and boastfulness and vainglory and contempt of other human beings, as if they themselves had accomplished something beyond human. How then would the Savior advise those who are going to live forever things that will harm and ruin them for the life which he promises? For again there is also that: a person is able, having unloaded his possession, nonetheless still to have the desire and the longing for money ingrained and living with him, and to have thrown away the use of it, but being at a loss and at the same time longing for what he squandered, to be grieved doubly, both by the absence of the service and by the presence of the repentance. For it is unattainable and impossible that one who needs the necessities for living should not have his judgment broken down and be led into distraction from better things, trying in some way and from some source to procure these things.

choices.why: The glossary and brief treat this as a fixed Pauline phrase; rendering it as 'new creation' preserves the theological term Clement is invoking.
The verb means to make naked; 'strip bare' keeps the physical force of the image, which Clement applies to the soul and disposition, not to possessions.
The adverb means 'from the roots'; the English idiom 'root and branch' conveys total removal and matches Clement's emphatic language.
The verb means to lay down a burden; 'unloaded' keeps the metaphor of possessions as a load, which Clement contrasts with the lingering desire.
The verb means to break or bend down; 'broken down' preserves the sense of the judgment being weakened or crushed by need.

pass_b_english: What then does he command as something new and proper to God, the only thing that makes alive, which did not save those who came before? If the new creation, the Son of God, reveals and teaches something exceptional, he is not commanding the outward thing that others have done, but something else signified through it, greater and more divine and more complete: to strip bare the soul itself and its disposition of the passions that underlie it, and to cut out and cast away root and branch the things alien to the judgment. For this is the lesson proper to the believer, and the teaching worthy of the Savior. Those who came before despised external things and let their possessions go and wasted them, but the passions of their souls, I think, they even increased. For they fell into arrogance and boastfulness and vainglory and contempt for other human beings, as if they themselves had done something beyond human. How then would the Savior advise those who are to live forever to avoid the things that harm and ruin them for the life he promises? And there is also this: a person can unload his possessions and nonetheless still have the desire and craving for money ingrained and living with him. He has thrown away the use of it, but being at a loss and at the same time longing for what he squandered, he is grieved twice over—both by the absence of the service it gave and by the presence of regret. For it is impossible and impracticable for someone who lacks the necessities for living not to have his judgment broken down and not to be drawn away from better things, trying to procure them somehow and from somewhere.

The source word μετανοίας here means regret or remorse in context, not the positive repentance of salvation; changed 'repentance' to 'regret'.

last_rejected.why: συνουσία means 'presence/companionship,' but μετάνοια here means 'regret' not 'repentance'; the grief is from regret, not from repentance being present.
last_rejected.fix: by the regret that remains with him
last_rejected.ruling: συνουσία = fellowship/association; "presence" is a minor nuance, not a meaning change; μετάνοια = repentance here, not merely regret.

last_rejected.why: κατακλάω means 'break, crush, subdue' in a negative sense of being overwhelmed/distressed, not 'broken down' as if destroyed; context shows distraction, not destruction of judgment.
last_rejected.fix: not to be crushed in spirit and distracted
last_rejected.ruling: κατακλᾶσθαι = to be crushed or broken; "broken down" conveys impairment of judgment, acceptable translation.

last_rejected.why: Greek says “of the mind,” not “of judgment,” altering the meaning.
last_rejected.ruling: γνώμη has wide semantic range including 'judgment,' 'mind,' 'purpose'; 'judgment' is valid rendering.
